'''Dimethyl oxalate''' is an [[organic compound]] with the formula {{chem2|(CO2CH3)2}} or {{chem2|(CH3)2C2O4}}. It is the [[methyl group|dimethyl]] [[ester]] of [[oxalic acid]]. Dimethyl oxalate is a colorless or white solid that is soluble in water.

==Production==
Dimethyl oxalate can be obtained by [[esterification]] of oxalic acid with [[methanol]] using [[sulfuric acid]] as a [[Catalysis|catalyst]]:<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.15227/orgsyn.010.0078|title=Methyl Oxalate|journal=Organic Syntheses|year=1930|volume=10|page=78|author=Everett Bowden}}</ref>
:<math>\rm 2\ CH_3OH + (CO_2H)_2\ \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4}\ (CO_2CH_3)_2 + 2\ H_2O</math>

===Oxidative carbonylation route===
The preparation by [[oxidative carbonylation]] has attracted interest because it requires only [[C1 Chemistry|C1 precursors]]:<ref>Hans-Jürgen Arpe: ''Industrielle Organische Chemie: Bedeutende Vor- und Zwischenprodukte'', S. 168; {{ISBN|978-3-527-31540-6}}.</ref>
:<math>\rm 4 \ CH_3OH + 4 \ CO + O_2 \xrightarrow{catalyst}\ 2 \ (CO_2CH_3)_2 + 2 \ H_2O</math>

The reaction is catalyzed by Pd<sup>2+</sup>.<ref>{{cite patent| country = US| number = 4467109| title = Process for Continuous preparation of diester of oxalic acid| gdate = 1983-05-19| fdate = 1984-08-21| inventor =Susumu Tahara et al.| assign1 = [[Ube Industries]]}} and {{cite patent| country = EP| number = 108359| title = Process for the preparation of a diester of oxalic acid| fdate = 1984-05-16| inventor = K. Masunaga et al.| assign1 = [[Ube Industries]]}}{{cite patent| country = EP| number = 425197| title = Process for preparing diester of carbonic acid| pubdate = 1991-05-2| invent1 = K. Nishihira| invent2 = K. Mizutare| assign1 = Ube Industries}}{{cite patent| country = US| number = 4451666| title = Synthesis of oxalate esters by the oxidative carbonylation of alcohols| pubdate = 1984-05-29| inventor =J.A. Sofranko, A.M. Gaffney| assign1 = Atlantic Richfield Co.}}</ref><ref name="Amadio">E. Amadio: [http://dspace.unive.it/bitstream/handle/10579/946/Amadio%20Emanuele_955382_thesis.pdf ''Oxidative Carbonylation of Alkanols Catalyzed by Pd(II)-Phosphine Complexes''], PhD Thesis, Ca'Foscari University Venice, 2009</ref> The synthesis gas is mostly obtained from [[coal]] or [[biomass]]. The oxidation proceeds via [[dinitrogen trioxide]], which is formed according to (1) of [[nitrogen monoxide]] and [[oxygen]] and then reacts according to (2) with methanol forming [[methyl nitrite]]:<ref name="Jiang">X.-Z. Jiang, ''Palladium Supported Catalysts in CO + RONO Reactions'', Platinum Metals Rev., 1990, '''34''', (4), 178–180</ref>

:[[File:Methylnitrite Synthesis.svg|Methylnitrit-Synthese]]

In the next step of dicarbonylation (3) [[carbon monoxide]] reacts with methyl nitrite to dimethyl oxalate in the vapor phase at atmospheric pressure and temperatures at 80-120 °C over a [[palladium]] catalyst:

:[[File:DMO Synthesis Summary.svg|DMO-Synthese zusammengefasst]]

The sum equation:

:[[File:DMO from MeOH via oxidative carbonylation.svg|DMO from MeOH via oxidative carbonylation]]
This method is lossless with respect to methyl nitrite, which acts practically as a carrier of oxidation equivalents. However, the water formed must be removed to prevent hydrolysis of the dimethyl oxalate product. With 1% Pd/α-Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> dimethyl oxalate is produced selectively in a dicarbonylation reaction, under the same conditions with 2% Pd/C dimethyl carbonate is produced by monocarbonylation:

:[[File:Monocarbonylation of MeOH corr.svg|Monocarbonylation of MeOH corr]]

Alternatively, the oxidative carbonylation of methanol can be carried out with high yield and selectivity with [[1,4-Benzoquinone|1,4-benzoquinone]] as an oxidant in the system [[Palladium(II) acetate|Pd(OAc)<sub>2</sub>]]/[[Triphenylphosphine|PPh<sub>3</sub>]]/benzoquinone with mass ratio 1/3/100 at 65 °C and 70 atm [[Carbon monoxide|CO]]:<ref name="Amadio" />

:[[File:Oxidative carbonylation with BQ corr.svg|Oxidative carbonylation with BQ corr]]

==Reactions==
Dimethyl oxalate (and the related diethyl ester) is used in diverse [[condensation reaction]]s.<ref name="Bergman">{{Cite journal|last1=Bergman|first1=Jan|last2=Norrby|first2=Per-Ola |last3=Sand|first3=Peter|date=1990|title=Alkylation with Oxalic Esters. Scope and mechanism|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0040402001879333|journal=Tetrahedron|language=en|volume=46|issue=17|pages=6113–6124|doi=10.1016/S0040-4020(01)87933-3|s2cid=94945519|issn=0040-4020|url-access=subscription}}</ref> For example, diethyl oxalate condenses with [[cyclohexanone]] to give the diketo-ester, a precursor to pimelic acid.<ref>{{cite journal|author=H. R. Snyder |author2=L. A. Brooks |author3=S. H. Shapiro |author4=A. Müller |title=Pimelic Acid|journal=Organic Syntheses|volume=11|page=42|year=1931|doi=10.15227/orgsyn.011.0042}}</ref> With diamines, the diesters of oxalic acid condense to give cyclic diamides. [[Quinoxalinedione]] is produced by condensation of dimethyloxalate and [[o-phenylenediamine]]:
:C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>(OMe)<sub>2</sub> + C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>(NH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>(NHCO)<sub>2</sub> + 2 MeOH

Hydrogenation gives [[ethylene glycol]].<ref>Nexant/Chemsystems, {{cite web |url=http://www.chemsystems.com/reports/search/docs/prospectus/stmc10_coal_meg.pdf |title=''Coal to MEG, Changing the Rules of the Game'' |access-date=2016-08-08 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110714135349/http://www.chemsystems.com/reports/search/docs/prospectus/stmc10_coal_meg.pdf |archive-date=July 14, 2011}} (PDF; 5,4 MB), 2011 Prospectus</ref> Dimethyl oxalate can be converted into ethylene glycol in high yields (94.7%)<ref>{{cite patent| country = EP| number = 046 983| title = Process for continuously preparing ethylene glycol| fdate = 1982-03-10| invent1 = S. Tahara et al.| assign1 = Ube Industries}} and H. T. Teunissen and C. J. Elsevier, ''Ruthenium catalyzed hydrogenation of dimethyl oxalate to ethylene glycol'', J. Chem. Soc., Chem. Commun., 1997, 667-668), [[DOI:10.1039/A700862G]].</ref><ref>S. Zhang et al., ''Highly-Dispersed Copper-Based Catalysts from Cu–Zn–Al Layered Double Hydroxide Precursor for Gas-Phase Hydrogenation of Dimethyl Oxalate to Ethylene Glycol'', Catalysis Letters, Sept. 2012, '''142''' (9), 1121–1127, [[DOI:10.1007/s10562-012-0871-8]]</ref>

:[[File:MEG from DMO.svg|MEG from DMO]]

The methanol formed is recycled in the process of oxidative carbonylation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.icis.com/resources/news/2012/01/30/9527520/china-s-coal-based-chemicals-are-a-trade-off/|title=Individual news}}</ref> Other plants with a total annual capacity of more than 1 million tons of ethylene glycol per year are planned.

Decarbonylation gives [[dimethyl carbonate]].<ref>{{cite patent| country = US| number = 4544507| title = Production of carbonate diesters from oxalate diesters| fdate = 1985-10-01| inventor =P. Foley| assign1 = Celanese Corp}}</ref>
:[[File:DMC from DMO.svg|DMC from DMO]]

Diphenyl oxalate is obtained by [[transesterification]] with [[phenol]] in the presence of titanium catalysts,<ref>{{cite patent| country = US| number = 5834614| title = Process for producing diaryl carbonate| fdate = 1998-11-10| inventor =K. Nishihira et al.| assign1 = Ube Industries, Ltd.}} and X.B. Ma et al., ''Preparation of Diphenyl Oxalate from Transesterification of Dimethyl Oxalate with Phenol over TS-1 Catalyst'', Chinese Chem. Lett., '''14''' (5), 461–464 (2003), [[DOI:10.1016/s0378-3820(03)00075-4]].</ref> which is again decarbonylated to [[diphenyl carbonate]] in the liquid or gas phase.

Dimethyl oxalate can also be used as a [[methylating agent]]. It is notably less toxic than other methylating agents such as [[methyl iodide]] or [[dimethyl sulfate]].<ref name="Bergman" />
